articles.title_orig: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.content_orig:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
after newsletter promotion
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

Ben is based in South Africa and also works on The Telegraph's Global Health Security team. He spent five years in Kabul covering the Afghanistan war, five years as Defence Correspondent in London, and four years in Islamabad
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.
The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.
“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.
“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.
The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.
Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.
Health unions have said staff should not be forced to put their lives at risk because of inadequate protective gear and have also raised concerns of short-staffing and a lack of preparedness in hospitals.
The Ebola virus is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood and saliva, and health workers or close relatives tending to the sick are particularly prone to getting infected themselves.
Dr Ibrahim Matende, president of the Kenya Medical Association, said: “Every healthcare worker deserves a safe working environment and timely access to the highest standard of care.”
The cases in Kenya have also raised questions about biosecurity and surveillance in the region after the index case – a Kenyan national living in eastern DRC – took flights and crossed international borders despite apparently becoming increasingly ill and showing Ebola-like symptoms.
The businessman had been unwell for two weeks when on October 1 he boarded a domestic flight from Kisangani to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has in recent weeks become one of the outbreak’s main hotspots.
Crossing over into Uganda, he then travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on October 3. Uganda has not reported any cases so far.
A relative collected him and drove him to the private Nairobi Hospital, while he was suffering with fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
He was confirmed to be infected with the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and died two days later.
Meanwhile, Africa’s top public health agency and Congolese officials have raised concerns that over $700 million in Ebola aid is unaccounted for, and called on aid groups to provide more information about their finances, Associated Press reported.
Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said last week that international donors had transferred close to a billion dollars to aid organisations in eastern DRC since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.
But only $200 million has been accounted for by international and local organisations working on the ground.
Only one-third of the organisations attended a recent meeting organised by Congo’s health ministry and provided their financial records, Dr Kaseya said.
Those attending said they received $228 million, of which $127 ⁠million had been spent and around $100 million remained available.
Dr Kaseya did not identify which organisations had not provided their records.
“This represents a significant lack of transparency and financial reporting on the part of these organisations, preventing the Government from having a comprehensive overview of the resources mobilised, how they were utilised and the results achieved,” the Africa CDC said.
“It is unacceptable for organisations to receive hundreds of millions of dollars to intervene in a country facing a major health emergency without providing a transparent account to the national authorities responsible for coordinating the response.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says China-aligned hackers used AI agents in ConnectWise attack
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says China-aligned hackers used AI agents in ConnectWise attack
articles.content_orig:
IB is seeking expert comment and will update this story as it develops
China-aligned hackers used an AI attack tool to break into a backup service used by IT providers, giving them a route into hundreds of businesses at once, Microsoft said on Wednesday.
For cyber insurers, it is the scenario they worry about most: one supplier, many victims.
In the report published yesterday, Microsoft blamed a group it calls Storm-0940 for the recent hack of ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. The group used ARTEX, a tool that lets AI agents run an attack from start to finish with little human input. Its developer took ARTEX closed source on 8 October after researchers linked it to attacks on South Korean banks, but copies already downloaded remain in circulation.
The speed stood out. Microsoft said the tool reached more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts a minute, “a pace that leaves defenders with little time to detect and respond”.
ConnectWise sells software to managed service providers (MSPs), the outsourced IT firms that run systems for many small businesses. Its backup tool has wide access to clients' email, files and Teams data.
According to Huntress , the attackers stole the tool's credential and on 15 October used it to log in to customer systems as the app itself, sidestepping passwords and multi-factor checks. Huntress confirmed unauthorised logins in 173 tenants as of 17 October, and says the real figure is likely higher.
In some cases, Microsoft said, the AI agents went further, changing credentials to keep access and altering admin roles. It has not said how many organisations were breached, and noted that a login does not always mean data was stolen. Targets included defence, energy, government, legal and financial services firms.
Read next: Perth arrests reveal the supply chain blind spot in Australian cyber cover
ConnectWise shut the service down on 17 October and completed a full reset of all accounts and credentials in the affected environment on 19 October, according to its security advisories. Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management all remain suspended. The company says it is preparing a phased restoration that will take several days once it begins, and that there is no sign backup data was taken.
One stolen credential opened a door into hundreds of unrelated businesses within hours. That is exactly where “widespread event” clauses and the policy definition of “computer system” come into play, and where having a policy does not always mean being covered.
AXA XL's Vicky Sheridan flagged the trend in Insurance Business's 2026 5-Star Cyber report : “We're also seeing growing exposure to cyber risks arising from third-party technology providers.”
The outage adds another layer. With backups still offline a week on, clients cannot restore data. Cover for a supplier's outage is often sublimited, and Allianz says cyber business interruption indemnity periods typically run just 90 to 180 days.
Read next: Australian firms face growing outage losses their insurance may not cover
Storm-0940 has been active since 2021. What is new is the pace. Microsoft says several hacking groups now use ARTEX, and executive vice president Igor Tsyganskiy called the ConnectWise attack “one of many” in a wave of AI-driven attacks since early October.
Costs were already climbing. The Australian Signals Directorate's Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25 found the average self-reported cybercrime cost for large businesses jumped 219% to $202,700 per report, though the ASD cautions that a drop in large-business reporting leaves that average exposed to outliers.
Read next: AI has changed the cyber threat. Has your clients' cover kept up?
Does the client's IT provider use ConnectWise Cloud Backup or SkyKick? If so, has it checked for suspicious logins since 13 October? If data was accessed, privacy notification rules and policy conditions apply, so tell the insurer early.
Then check the wording. Does the policy cover a breach that started in a supplier's software? Is contingent business interruption included, and at what limit? Could a systemic event clause apply?
Brokers and insurers should ask the same questions of their own IT providers.
There is an irony here. ConnectWise has long promoted itself as a path to cyber cover for MSPs, partnering in 2022 with broker Ukon (formerly FifthWall Solutions), which said it worked with more than 35 insurers. The question now is whether those policies were written for a week like this.

articles.title_orig: EU’s idea that China is caving to pressure is ‘serious misjudgment’: ex-diplomat
articles.title_zh: EU’s idea that China is caving to pressure is ‘serious misjudgment’: ex-diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Brussels has been emboldened by recent hybrid car deal, but China will not back down in the face of trade pressure, former diplomat warns
The European Union’s perception that China is yielding to its pressure tactics on trade is a “serious misjudgment”, as Beijing proved during last year’s tariff war with the United States that it will not back down from a confrontation, a former Chinese diplomat has warned.
But in reality, China only acted out of a willingness to safeguard its vast bilateral economic ties with Europe, and further provocations could backfire on the EU, according to Cui Hongjian, who served as a diplomat in India and Jamaica during the 2000s.
“China’s willingness to reach agreements with the EU on electric vehicle export restrictions and other issues is not because we fear Europe, nor because we only respond to pressure,” said Cui, who now serves as director of the Centre for EU and Regional Development Studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X .
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used.  Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.

articles.title_orig: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
articles.title_zh: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
articles.content_orig:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The September jobs report will be released Nov. 5.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

Published: 08:00 EDT, 21 October 2026 | Updated: 06:53 EDT, 22 October 2026

After months of anticipation, Apple finally unveiled its first foldable iPhone last month – the iPhone Duo.
The device folds open like a book, transforming from a regular–sized smartphone into a mini tablet, with a bigger screen for multitasking, watching videos and getting things done.
But is it just a £2,000 gimmick, or is it finally time to embrace the dual–screen life?
The iPhone Duo goes on sale this Friday, October 23, with pre–orders already selling out.
However, the Daily Mail's Science & Technology Editor, Shivali Best, was among the first to get her hands on the device and has spent the past week putting it through its paces.
If you're simply looking for a new smartphone, Apple's flagship iPhone 18 Pro may be the better choice. It boasts a more advanced camera system and starts at £1,199 – £800 less than the Duo.
But if you regularly switch between your phone and a tablet, the Duo could be the perfect hybrid device you've been waiting for.
After months of anticipation, Apple finally unveiled its first foldable iPhone last month – the iPhone Duo
The device folds open like a book, transforming from a regular–sized smartphone into a mini tablet, with a bigger screen for multitasking, watching videos and getting things done
Ahead of its launch, rumours were flying left, right and centre about the design for the foldable iPhone.
In the end, Apple opted for a book–style design, with a 5.4–inch outer display, and a 7.6–inch inner folding display.
While this sounds like it might be clunky, in practice, it's absolutely stunning.
When it's closed, the iPhone Duo has a wider, shorter design than a standard iPhone, with a straight edge down the left–hand–side, and curved corners on the right.

Colours : Star White, Night Sky

Inner display : 7.6–inch Super Retina XDR folding display

Crucially, I can confirm that it slides into both the front and back pockets of a women's pair of jeans with ease – something that prospective buyers have raised concerns about across social media.
Having tested various other foldable smartphones, I half expected to be greeted by a dreaded crease down the middle of the iPhone Duo when I opened it up.
However, Apple has managed to avoid this much–hated feature by opting for a nano–texture finish on the inner screen.
This finish creates a matte surface that minimises crease visibility and reduces glare.
It's noticeably different to most iPhones, and does take some getting used to, but I really like it – it feels lovely to the touch, and will make using the device in bright sunshine much easier.
The opened screen is also impressively thin, measuring just 5.2mm thick, making it even thinner than last year's iPhone Air.
One feature that did slightly irritate me, however, is the fact that the iPhone Duo does not lay flat when the screen is fully open, thanks to the raised rear camera bump.
When you're trying to type with the smartphone laid on a flat surface, the whole thing rocks backwards and forwards, making a knocking noise in the process.
You can rectify this by folding it to a right angle and just typing on one side, but if you prefer typing across a full–screen keyboard, this could be an issue.
When it's closed, the iPhone Duo has a wider, shorter design than a standard iPhone, with a straight edge down the left–hand–side, and curved corners on the right
The outer screen's display looks much like a standard iPhone at first glance – but there are some key differences.
To compensate for the shorter screen, Apple has moved the dock from the bottom to the right–hand side of the screen.
On the homescreen, this isn't really an issue, although I do find myself second guessing where my Phone, Messages and Camera app are from time–to–time.
What's more, Apple has optimised the layout of its own native apps so they fit the entire screen.
However, where this becomes a problem is when using non–native apps.
Opening up TikTok – one of my most–used apps – I was disappointed to discover an unsightly black bar down the right–hand side of the screen, which is fairly distracting while you're scrolling through your feed.
Other popular apps are plagued with the same issue, with Outlook also displaying the same black bar.
I'm sure these apps will optimise their layouts for the unusual screen size over time, but at the moment it makes using your favourites rather jarring.
Having the dock on the right–hand–side also makes the iPhone tricky to use for left–handers.
When closed, you can just about stretch your left thumb across to the dock, but when the iPhone Duo is open, even people with enormous hands will struggle to reach it.
Another feature that definitely takes some getting used to is Touch ID, which lets you unlock the iPhone Duo using a side button.
If you're a selfie fan, you'll be happy to hear that there are three different ways to snap photos of yourself
If you'd prefer to use the rear camera, you can turn the unfolded device around and snap a selfie, with a preview shown on the opposite side
With Apple using its facial recognition system, Face ID, in iPhones since 2017, I can't help but feel like this is a backwards step.
I'm sure you'd get used to it eventually, but during my week with the iPhone Duo, I often found myself staring at the screen, wondering why it wouldn't simply unlock by scanning my face.
Opening up the screen, I really like the transition from the front display to the inner one.
As you slowly open it up, the front screen begins to blur while the inner screen fades into view, bringing whatever content you were looking at on the closed device across to the main screen.
However, the opening process itself isn't exactly smooth, and it takes quite a bit of force to pry it open with two hands.
I tried opening it with one hand and it was a real struggle – while doing a dramatic, 90s–style slam shut will also leave you unsatisfied.
Where the iPhone Duo really shines is in Split View mode, in which you can have two apps running side–by–side.
This is hugely helpful for those situations where you need information from two sources at the same time.
If you see it is an iPhone/iPad hybrid, you might be able to justify the price to yourself

For example, I needed to transfer money to a friend, who had sent me her bank details over on WhatsApp.
Instead of flicking back and forth between my banking app and WhatsApp as I entered her details, I simply opened both apps at the same time and tapped in the Sort Code and Account Number without fuss.
Meanwhile, while replying to an email asking about my availability for a meeting, I could get my calendar up on the other side of the screen, rather than flicking between the two.
While this makes juggling tasks much easier, concerns have been raised on social about how Split View might fuel 'brain rot'.
Several previous studies have linked heavy media multitasking with poorer attention in some groups, although the evidence is mixed.
The iPhone Duo has four cameras – two rear lenses (a 48MP main camera and a 8MP ultra–wide camera), one 12MP selfie camera on the front of the device, and an under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen.
This might be disappointing if you've previously used one of the Pro iPhones.

As a longtime user of the original, Neil was excited to see what the new COROS DURA 2 SOLAR had in store. His review dives into his impressions of the new head unit, how it differs from the much-beloved debut model, and whether the price jump is worth it for those considering the upgrade. Find his full video and written reviews below…
Additional photos by Logan Watts
Today, we’re looking at a new head unit, the COROS DURA 2 SOLAR. It looks unlike any I’ve ever seen. In my latest review, I’ll be diving into the details you need to know, including the specs, some interesting new features, a few major head-scratchers, and my first impressions. Check out my full video review followed by a written version below.
The original DURA was, and still is, an amazing head unit. It has the best battery life of any head unit I’ve ever used, a simple interface in a sea of increasingly complicated options, and, best of all, a very affordable $250 price tag. COROS made a splash in the cycling world, and the DURA became one of the best head units for bikepacking. In fact, I’ll say it: for trips longer than three days, it’s my first choice because of its battery life. Before the first DURA release, COROS wasn’t exactly a household name in cycling. Despite its success, it still might not be a household name. But it gained plenty of recognition for delivering a head unit that lasts a ridiculously long time without breaking the bank, giving it a solid foothold in a saturated industry.
That said, COROS released the first DURA before it was truly ready. Maybe that’s why the price tag was so enticing. Did it get the job done? Yes. But as I mentioned in my *original review*, there were some hiccups. I held off on reviewing it until a few firmware updates had addressed enough of those issues. Doing a first look at the DURA 2 SOLAR hurts a little, because I know I haven’t put it through the kind of testing I normally would for a full review. But most of those early growing pains seem to be behind us. And during my initial testing, the DURA 2 has felt much more refined and ready for market. And yes, it’s pretty darn weird-looking.
The unit comes in a nice box. Open it up, and you’ll find the DURA 2 SOLAR with stickers identifying the dials and buttons. It also comes with a lanyard to wrap around the bars or stem for security, which I always use with head units. I appreciate that COROS still includes what looks like a quality, long USB-C to USB-C cable and a bunch of instructions. Oddly enough, my test unit didn’t come with a mount. Logan got the new aluminum one, and he said it’s well-made and sleek, and it comes with a GoPro-style undermount option for lights or a camera.
Since plenty of customers already have mounts, you can buy the unit on its own or pay extra for a version with a mount. I asked COROS to send me one, but it didn’t arrive in time. Packaging isn’t a major factor in the overall experience of any piece of tech, but it’s well done here: clean, nearly all recyclable, and thoughtfully put together. Many cycling head unit companies have dialed that in over the last few years, and I appreciate it.
The DURA 2 SOLAR is a big departure from the original unit. The original unit positioned itself as a budget option amid increasingly expensive computers. I don’t know if this was the plan all along, but bringing an affordable head unit into a market with so few budget options made a lot of sense. Add the incredible battery life, and the original DURA was a unicorn. But breaking into the cycling industry as a relatively unknown brand isn’t easy. COROS mentioned that DURA sales were a little slow at first, but picked up as more people learned about the price and user feedback and reviews started rolling in.
Instead of updating the DURA and maintaining that price point, COROS decided to go premium. I’ll admit it’s a little disappointing, especially since they’re discontinuing the original. I’m sad to see that option go, and it feels like a massive miss. Let’s hope they bring a lower-budget option to the table, but I’m not holding my breath. If anything, I think they might drop “SOLAR” from the product name and launch a non-solar unit at a slightly lower price, but that would eliminate one of the new unit’s best features.
I’ve always thought of COROS as a brand for the people. I’ve used their watches for three years now, and between the features, battery life, and price, they’re pretty hard to beat. It gave me the impression that a brand could build good products, deliver a strong user experience, and still make a profit without charging top dollar. That said, the DURA 2 SOLAR comes in at $499 without a mount or $549 with one. That puts the unit alone at roughly twice the price of the first DURA, which launched just two years ago. Inflation aside, that’s a pretty big jump. So, let’s dive into the differences and see whether the new one is worth it.
The new DURA 2 SOLAR is a looker. It uses a carbon-and-alloy construction, compared to the first DURA’s mostly plastic body, and they weigh about the same: 100 grams for the DURA 2 SOLAR and 101 grams for the other. The overall shape is strange. It almost looks like a concept car, and COROS seems to be leaning into aerodynamics. The upper portion is only 5.7mm thick, easily the thinnest of any head unit I’ve tested. It thickens toward the main body near the quarter-turn mount. It’s similar in width to the original but significantly longer, measuring 117mm long, 58mm wide, and 17mm thick. Overall, it feels nice in the hand and is fairly lightweight. Once you attach it to the quarter-turn mount, it sits nicely out front. From the top, it doesn’t look nearly as ridiculous as it does from the side.
The controls have changed too. It has two physical buttons, one on each side, but the oversized watch-style scroll dial is gone, which I really enjoyed using. Now you get two haptic buttons at the bottom, plus an updated touchscreen that feels much more sensitive and responsive than the original. You can also charge the device using the USB-C port below the right button. The larger 3.5” display is a welcome change. This was one of my complaints with the original, especially when navigating: it seemed like they could have fit a larger screen into the body. I think they’ve done a good job addressing that here. In my initial testing, the touchscreen works well, and I like the haptic feedback. And paired with the side buttons, it’s intuitive and relatively simple to use.
Speaking of the screen, the DURA 2 SOLAR still uses a sunlight-readable, Memory-in-Pixel, or MIP, display designed for low power consumption. Howeve

The world's richest man confirmed this week that Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, the companies are worth about $3.5 trillion (€3.1tn), making it potentially the biggest merger ever.
It would cap a string of deals tying Elon Musk's businesses together, and the goal is to complete it while Donald Trump is still the US president, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be the latest chapter in a story that began a decade ago, when Musk started stitching his companies together.
In 2016, Tesla bought SolarCity , a solar panel installer run by his cousins, a deal that was only upheld by a Delaware court after years of litigation.
In March 2025, his AI start-up xAI swallowed X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, which Musk acquired for $44 billion (€39.1bn) in 2022.
In February this year, SpaceX absorbed xAI , in a deal that valued the rocket maker at $1 trillion (€890bn) and the AI firm at $250 billion (€222bn), ahead of SpaceX's initial public offering (IPO).
Four months later, SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq, raising $85.7 billion (€76.3bn) in the biggest stock market debut in history.
Seen together, the deals look like part of a long-running plan to fold Musk's businesses into one publicly traded group. Musk himself spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on an earnings call in July.
On Tuesday, Musk told analysts on SpaceX's earnings call that both companies had set up committees of independent board members to study a merger. He called it "a good idea", while admitting he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield".
Musk argues that AI will decide where both companies go next.
They are already jointly developing Terafab , an AI chip factory in Texas, while Tesla's driverless cars and Optimus humanoid robots could benefit from the computing power SpaceX is racing to build, including planned data centres in orbit.
SpaceX posted its first quarterly profit since listing, earning $4.4 billion (€3.9bn) as revenue jumped 161%, but its capital spending reached $19.6 billion (€17.4bn) in the quarter, mostly on AI.
By contrast, a day later, Tesla reported that its net profit fell 43% to $787 million (€700mn) on flat revenue of $28 billion (€24.9bn), as deliveries slipped 2%. In a combined company, SpaceX's surging revenue could help offset Tesla's figures.
Merging the businesses would also allow Musk to run all their operations under one roof, moving engineers and resources between the companies without disclosures or lawsuits over related-party deals.
Control is another potential benefit.
Musk owns about 48% of SpaceX and holds more than 80% of its votes through special shares, but only about 20% of Tesla. Since 2024, Musk has said he is uncomfortable turning Tesla into an AI and robotics leader without at least 25% of the votes.
A merger could also make him richer, as his Tesla pay package treats many of its performance goals as achieved if certain types of mergers go through.
Reportedly, the aim is to announce a merger deal in the first half of 2027 and complete it before US President Donald Trump's term ends in January 2029, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
Completing the deal while Trump is in office could give it a friendlier political reception, although it would still face regulatory and shareholder scrutiny.
Musk, who led Trump's cost-cutting drive in 2025 before a public falling-out , has since made up with the US president and returned to the administration.
He has also become the biggest known donor supporting Republican candidates in next month's US midterm elections, giving more than $276 million (€245mn) since July, according to a spokesperson for America PAC, Musk's conservative super PAC.
A Democratic win could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX's federal contracts and Tesla's self-driving software.
SpaceX itself warned in its listing documents that a shift in power in Congress could have a "material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position".
The committees have yet to agree on terms, and any deal would need the backing of more than half of all Tesla shares, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle". He cautioned that a merger was not certain.
Tesla shareholders meet on 3 December.

A majority of Americans view artificial intelligence as a threat to broader society, even as half believe the technology delivers personal benefits to their daily lives, according to a nationwide ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released Wednesday.
The poll revealed 57% of adults say AI is bad for society overall, compared to 42% who see it as a societal good.
A majority of Republicans (57%) say AI is personally good for them while a similar majority of Democrats say it's personally bad for them (55%), marking a contrast between the majority political parties before the midterms.
The survey reveals key partisan and generational divides over tech adoption. While 63% of Democrats and 58% of independents view AI's societal impact negatively, Republicans lean more favorable, with 51% calling it beneficial overall.
Anti-progressive anxiety remains centered on widespread job displacement, cybersecurity risks, and economic inequality, alongside broad opposition to the local expansion of energy-intensive AI data centers powering the underlying infrastructure.
Anthropic is pressing forward with plans for a mid-November initial public offering (IPO), standing as the sole major AI firm remaining on a fall tech calendar otherwise emptied by rising interest rates and market volatility.
The AI lab is expected to make its prospectus public as early as late October and begin marketing shares to prospective investors during the week of Nov. 9.
Anthropic's listing will test whether its central role in the AI sector – where it is eyeing a valuation of up to $1.5 trillion – can overcome broader market headwinds.
Rising interest rates and growing skepticism around massive data center expenditures have forced peers to pull or delay their listings.
CoreWeave has suffered a steep selloff in shares and bonds, while infrastructure providers including Switch, Nscale, SB Energy, Elice, AirTrunk REIT, and Firmus have all paused or postponed their public offerings.

"The reason why I'm not sure is because I don't think anybody in Congress really fully understands the dangers of AI ," Hamilton, a pastor and founder of the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, argued.
Leaving AI oversight to tech companies is a "bad idea," he added, calling on Congress to enlist industry experts to prevent threats to future generations.
Incumbent opponent Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., advocated for a "light touch" regulatory approach focused on national security, domestic privacy, and staying ahead of China.
Marshall pushed back against broad global regulatory frameworks, warning that adversarial nations like Russia and China would never abide by international rules that Democrats and globalists push.

Under the agreement, the federal government will receive minority, non-controlling equity stakes in exchange for the capital injection.
Drawn from a $10 billion R&D fund established by Congress in 2022 , the awards target next-generation chip technology for fusion power, AI hardware, and raw material purification.
Helion will receive up to $175 million for fusion-generator semiconductors, while Commonwealth Fusion Systems is slated for up to $85 million. articles.title_orig: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.title_zh: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.content_orig:
Even though I was born in the Apollo Era, barely, the spacecraft that I think had the most influence on my childhood had to be the Space Shuttles. I remember poring over diagrams and drawings of the shuttles in National Geographic foldouts, where they even took my attention from the Forbidden Nipples seen on some of the other pages. I remember watching that first launch of the shuttle Colombia in 1981, I remember the tragedy of the Challenger in 1986, and I remember covering the process of moving the orbiter Endeavour through the streets of Los Angeles to its eventual home at the California Science Center. And more recently, I’ve taken my kid to see the orbiter Discovery at the Udvar-Hazy Center just outside of Washington, DC.
It’s that orbiter that I want to talk about specifically, because I saw a social media post about the orbiter Discovery that grabbed my attention and held it with the sort of fierce grip I imagine Miss Piggy employs on Kermit’s impossibly thin limbs when they’re alone.
That post was on Threads, and I just figured out how to embed a post from that site, so here, you can see it for yourself:
Wait, what? Discovery has an upside-down ‘s’ in its name? How the hell did that happen? Discovery was usually considered, by astronauts and NASA people, the jewel in the Space Shuttle crown. It was recognized to be the most reliable and best-performing of all the orbiters, and had the most missions and time in space . Since it was first launched in 1984, Discovery completed 39 missions, spent in total a full year in space, and traveled 150 million miles.
The thing flew for 27 years, and somehow nobody noticed that the ‘s’ was upside down on the starboard side name text?
I mean, I guess I should be more understanding; I’ve seen it several times and never noticed, and it wasn’t until just tonight that I looked back at some old photos I took of Discovery the last time I was there and saw, holy crap, the dude on Threads was right. That ‘s’ is rotated 180°.
Now, the typography on the shuttle orbiters follows NASA’s carefully-planned and strictly-enforced graphic and typographic guidelines , which state that the typography used on the spacecraft should be Helvetica Medium:
Okay, let’s take a look at the typography on the orbiter:
(the ‘r’ on the font I used there feels a bit different, too, but this gets the point across and I have to get on a flight in a few hours so I’m gonna let that slide)
It’s a subtle difference, but as you can see, the starboard side’s name definitely has that flipped ‘s.’ It’s subtle, but the Helvetica ‘s’ is slightly wider on the bottom, giving the letter a somewhat more settled appearance. Here, look:
You can see the difference there, right? I feel like once it’s pointed out, you can’t help but notice it. The ‘v’ on the port side looks oddly thick, too, now that I’m looking at it.
I’ve been told that the graphics on these orbiters was applied using large stencils and special space-grade paint, and I’m sure the complex curves of the fuselage didn’t make the application of these elements easy. It’s understandable that a letter stencil may have been flipped around, but I am sort of surprised it was never corrected in its 27 years of service life.
All the other graphics and typography are applied with impressive precision; maybe there were people who knew that ‘s’ was wrong, but kind of liked that subtle imperfection, as it does add character to the spacecraft. I get that, absolutely. If I was in charge, I’d have just let it ride, too.
I still can’t believe I’d never clocked this before; as a typographic geek and a space geek who has spent far too much time looking at pictures of spacecraft in books and online, you’d think I’d have encountered this before, but, nope. Or if I did, it didn’t make enough of an impression to consciously note it or remember.
But now that it’s there? I can’t unsee it. And I’m sort of delighted by that.
Kerning around the v looks a little tight on the port side
Good type design is such a lost art… probably because it’s a tremendous ass-pain.
Thanks for posting the screenshot, whatever you embedded did not show up for me.
My first job out of college was with an aerospace company and we made some Shuttle parts.   Fantastic way to start out and still the most technically demanding job I’ve had.
Dude. I wonder if this was a deliberate move by a fellow Sid to sneak his name in upside-down and backwards on a space shuttle. If so, much respect.
This is now my favorite Shuttle Discovery fact. Those human touches on one of our greatest space-faring achievements really make it feel more humble. Kind of like how the letters just look spray painted on in general. Love that old space-based moving van.
Wow, that’s quite a discovery.
If NASA was actually a real government organization, they would have got this right in the first place. Since it’s obvs Hollywood built – let’s just call it what it is: a simple continuity error.
next thing you’ll tell me the “o” in Apollo was upside down as well???
rotated 37.7% actually – thanks for asking
All I have to say about this is that I initially misread the headline as A Typography Greek and I kinda like that better that way, too.
My first read was exactly the same.
The Udvar-Hazy museum is an absolute gem. Highly, highly recommended for any gearhead.
Wow. As a 25 year veteran sign guy, I can’t believe I never caught that either. I’ve handled I don’t know how many sets of Gemini letters, and it’s plainly obvious there’s a right-side-up when you’re holding the letter in your hand. I guess the odd curvature of the ship right there disguises it.
And now that I look more closely, that panel break cutting through the letters at an angle bugs me, too.
This really proves NASA did it…
When looking from the tarmac, the top part is further up and at an angle. Has to be bigger to optically match the bottom part that we’re looking at at a sharper angle.
Michelangelo’s David of fuselage ornamentation.
I was thinking the exact same thing…it makes the most sense.
The only hole in your theory is that the ‘s’ is not flipped on the port side where it is farther up on sloped area near the windscreen.
Don’t touch it, it was the good luck charm for the ship.
“fierce grip I imagine Miss Piggy employs on Kermit’s impossibly thin limbs when they’re alone.”
Did y’all know that James Hetfield of Metallica officiated the wedding of Kermit and Ms Piggy?
Makes sense because he’s the pastor of Muppets.
You got me.  I love you for that.
Working lightly in a similar field, I doubt the S would have had its own separate stencil.  It would have made more sense to have the entire word spelled out.
I wonder if there are pictures of the shuttle in the paint booth?
I’m guessing the reason most of us don’t notice is the angle at which we see it combining with the curve of the craft. It’s a subtle enough issue that those things absolutely mask the problem.
But now that you’ve mentioned it, I will never unsee it.
In space, nobody can hear you scream about typography errors.
There is no up or down in space.
Cue the “but the S used to be right-side up” Mandela-effect conspiracy theorists…

The thing re-entered the atmosphere 39 times ; it makes sense that NASA re-sprayed it at least once at some point.

articles.title_orig: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.title_zh: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.content_orig:
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

articles.title_zh: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
articles.content_orig:
American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.
Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.
"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.
Membership points vary by card:
The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer , a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

articles.title_orig: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.title_zh: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.content_orig:
A Mexican teenager died after falling from a carnival ride, with horrific video showing her flying out of her seat as the ride reached full speed.
Gabriela Rodriguez Tezoco, 18, died on Tuesday night following the accident at a festival in Los Cabos, Baja California Sur, local outlet Expreso reported .
Cell phone footage taken by another rider shows Tezoco plummeting to the ground from “The Pendulum,” a spinning ride at the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals.
Other riders could be heard screaming as the teenager fell off while the ride kept spinning at high speed.
Emergency services rushed to treat Tezoco, who was taken to a nearby hospital, where she sadly died from her injuries early Wednesday morning.
“It is with deep sorrow that we report that the young woman who was injured in the incident that occurred in the amusement park area of ​​the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals, and who was immediately transferred to receive medical attention, lost her life despite the efforts of the health personnel,” the Los Cabos City Council wrote on social media.
“The Pendulum” ride was closed in the wake of the incident while safety tests are carried out on it and the other attractions at the fair, Los Cabos mayor Christian Agundez told local reporters.
“Today, with the same spirit with which we come together to celebrate, we must come together to support Gabriela’s family. It could have been any one of us. You are not alone,” Agundez said during an appearance at a concert which was part of the festival.
An investigation has been opened both into the circumstances and to determine potential liability, the Baja California Sur State Attorney General’s Office reported on Wednesday.
So far, no arrests have been made, and no one responsible for the ride’s operation has been publicly identified.
Tezoco had just graduated this summer from the Baja California Sur College of Baccalaureate Studies.
“May your smile remain alive in our memory and may your memory always be a light that guides us,” the school said in a tribute.

articles.title_zh: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast .
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island , which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran  prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz —  cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”
Using tribal power and rigorous detective work, a family of an army officer in Yemen tries to find out how he was abducted in broad daylight, and what happened to him afterward.
In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.
In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.
Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.
The U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran was billed as the final blow to Tehran’s ‘Axis of Resistance,’ but the alliance though bloodied is unexpectedly resilient.
One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim’s residents.

articles.title_orig: What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
articles.title_zh: What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
articles.content_orig:
Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities
Hamas has warned Israel that it is prepared to carry out another attack similar to the October 7, 2023, assault wherever an opportunity arises, according to a Ynet report.
The reported threat extended to attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities.
According to Ynet, Alakbarov passed the warning to Maj. Gen. Yoram Halevy, the coordinator of government activities in the territories, during a meeting on Wednesday. A document outlining the threats was then urgently circulated to senior political and security officials.
Israeli officials reportedly described the warning as unusually explicit and severe.
During their meeting with Alakbarov, Hamas officials reportedly complained about developments they said were weakening the group’s hold on Gaza.
These included continued Israeli military operations, changes to the “yellow line” marking IDF positions, and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s cancellation of elections scheduled for November 28.
According to Ynet’s account, the Hamas representatives said they were no longer willing to accept the current situation.
The warning comes as Israeli forces continue to target Hamas operatives in Gaza, including commanders and members of the group’s Nukhba unit.
Meanwhile, the Peace Council and international mediators are pressing Hamas to surrender its weapons. Israeli assessments cited by Ynet suggest the group is seeking to draw out negotiations without committing to disarmament.
Israel, for its part, has refused to allow a proposed technocratic governing committee or a Palestinian police force into Gaza, leaving arrangements for the territory’s administration and security unresolved.

articles.title_orig: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.title_zh: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.content_orig:
Government and company websites around the world briefly went dark and suspended some services, as operators scrambled to patch their systems after artificial intelligence helped find critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language.
Nearly three dozen UK government services are unavailable and four are “partially unavailable” while security upgrades take place, UK government minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords Thursday. “No large public-facing critical services are being affected by the exercise but some limited services may temporarily be offline while security work is carried out,” a UK government spokesperson told reporters.
The US National Security Agenc y and Europe’s cybersecurity agency have advised companies to take immediate action to address two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers 70% of all websites in the world, including WordPress and Drupal, an open-source content management system.
The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language, has released a patch for the bugs, which have been hidden in their software for years, and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately.
Popular Irish news website The Journal was temporarily offline Thursday morning while it bolstered its “defences,” it said in a notice. The Journal is Ireland’s second most-used online news source, behind only RTÉ, the national broadcaster, according to the Reuters Institute.
The flaws in PHP – which originally stood for Personal Home Page – were uncovered by teams at OpenAI , Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif . The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to hack into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
“With PHP behind such a vast share of the web, the exposure could reach almost everywhere people spend money online,” said Nigel Green, the CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.
“Booking platforms, marketplaces, subscription services, ticketing sites, delivery apps and utility portals could all be holding card details on systems built with the same kind of code,” he added.
Even world leaders urged organizations to take action. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that his cabinet was “closely monitoring the situation surrounding the vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said companies should consider suspending services if necessary in order to reduce their exposure. “Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix patch that will be released tonight… as soon as possible,” she posted on X Wednesday.
Japanese airline ANA, railway operator JR West and the country’s largest bank, MUFG, were among companies that reported some webpages and services temporarily suspended.
In Europe, government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were temporarily taken offline while security fixes were implemented.
The Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit that operates Wikipedia, told CNN Thursday that it was “in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in PHP,” and that a number of its systems had been taken down as a “precautionary measure.”
AI played a crucial role in finding and fixing vulnerabilities “that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade,” according to Wiz, which said the episode marks an “AI inflection point.”
“What AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post Wednesday in which they described PHP as a “backbone of the web.”
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” they added.
The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public only on Wednesday, after PHP had come up with a fix.
The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue.
Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process.
Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected.
Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” the researchers said.
“Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
– CNN’s John Liu, Anna Cooban, Amy Croffey and James Frater contributed reporting.
