articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.content_orig:
From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout, millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.
“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.
Irina, who like several other people did not want her last name shared while she was speaking with a foreign news organization about a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians .
The disruption hit myriad services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia and whose digital infrastructure other third-party platforms rely on.
Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order taxis or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.
Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.
Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.
“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.
“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”
Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.
She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”
Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.
She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.
Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.
Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had been on the job for only a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July .
When the Yandex outages started, he said, the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer.
While that has been largely resolved, said Valery, 24, the biggest issue for him was that he could not withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” he said.
In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and the tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days.
The chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, a British think tank, told NBC News.
The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war.
Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast said, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning.
Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support, because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but it is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said.
On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers.
Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify whether Yandex services’ going down had that effect.
While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were easier targets, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network.
While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transportation, internet access and payments.
“Very easy and very important,” he said.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Youth-Led Protests Sweep Across Europe
articles.title_zh: Youth-Led Protests Sweep Across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable
L ast Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central France was set ablaze . By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, and other scenes of unrest across France , were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.
For some, the flames announced a pan-European youth revolt , proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but about migration and Islam , urged Europeans to “close the borders”. The mayor of Limoges saw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.
I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading across Europe , driven by the same grievances and violence.
None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.
What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France, the mobilisation began in schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances had widened to encompass the cost of living .
In Belgium, meanwhile , students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours. Greek students have mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, while German pupils have protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
Look beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. In Albania, student unrest builds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. In Serbia , students have led nearly two years of largely peaceful protests following the Novi Sad railway station disaster . Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students are running in this weekend’s election on their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.
Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images, slogans and tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.
Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain. Eurostat reports that EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026 TUI Foundation Youth Study found that 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.
Youth unemployment in the euro area remains substantially higher than overall unemployment. One study of French firms found a sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. The European Central Bank cautions that the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.
Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.
France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.
What happened in Milan showed how the two can blur . A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform, was followed by looting carried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence and scrutiny of police conduct .
But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.
after newsletter promotion
The misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.
This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.
For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, from the Trump administration to Vladimir Putin.
President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.
Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.
Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.

Today, Google and Voltus announced an expanded agreement to build a 1-gigawatt (GW) virtual power plant across the PJM grid region, which serves 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C.
Voltus aggregates flexible capacity from local businesses and homes — like smart thermostats, batteries, and industrial assets — into a Google-funded virtual power plant. During peak demand, these assets temporarily reduce energy use to support grid reliability. In return, participating customers receive direct economic benefits, including bill savings and cash payments.
Building on a 100-megawatt agreement from earlier this year, this 10-fold expansion represents one of the largest known distributed capacity portfolios deployed by a hyperscaler to date.
This initiative reflects Google’s commitment to actively bring new capacity to local grids while strengthening regional reliability and affordability.

articles.title_orig: Late detection in Nigeria raises alarm as Ebola spreads across Africa
articles.title_zh: Late detection in Nigeria raises alarm as Ebola spreads across Africa
articles.content_orig:
The World Health Organization warned on Thursday that Africa faced a "complex" Ebola outbreak after the virus crossed from east Africa to Nigeria, which has reported the first case in the west of the continent.
Nigeria on Tuesday announced an imported case of the Bundibugyo strain behind a major DR Congo Ebola outbreak, in a woman, a wife of a diplomat who had a history of travel to Uganda.
The continent's most populous nation is the fourth African country affected by the outbreak, which this week came to span the continent, with Kenya in the east reporting nine cases since October 6.
The outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of Congo and has become the deadliest in the country's history, killing more than 4,000 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since mid-May, according to health authorities.
It is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.
"We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape. Nigeria has confirmed an imported case of Ebola virus disease," Mohamed Janabi, regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing.
The patient in Nigeria returned to the capital Abuja on October 3 after being in Uganda since September 16, the WHO representative in Nigeria Pavel Ursu said.
She flew to Abuja on an Ethiopian Airlines flight and transited through Addis Ababa, an emergency meeting of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) heard on Wednesday.
The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya told AFP on Thursday.
He also said she did not go to the DRC, as suggested earlier by Ugandan authorities.
- 'Extremely serious threat' -
Africa CDC's Kaseya has already warned of "an extremely serious threat", with fatality rates fast edging towards 50 percent in the DRC.
The Nigerian case has reignited memories of a widespread outbreak in 2014 that struck several countries in the region and killed more than 11,000 people across west Africa between late 2013 and 2016.
Nigeria successfully contained the Ebola outbreak in 2014, resulting in only 19 infections and seven deaths, raising confidence it can respond effectively to new public health threats.
Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years.
In August, Uganda was declared officially Ebola-free by the WHO after recording 20 cases -- almost all of them in people who had travelled from the DRC.
Uganda has pushed back against suggestions the patient in Nigeria might have contracted the virus in the country.
"It's preposterous to suggest that just because someone was holidaying in Uganda, which by the way has no cases of Ebola, is reason enough to drag us into a conversation about Ebola in Nigeria," Ugandan government spokesman Alan Kasujja told AFP.
"We're trying as much as possible to make sure that Uganda is not branded as an Ebola country," he added.
The WHO representative in Nigeria said patient zero, who is receiving treatment at a private hospital, was showing "positive signs".
An NCDC official said a day earlier that she had experienced multiple organ failure.

articles.title_orig: German youth plan France-style mass protests
articles.title_zh: German youth plan France-style mass protests
articles.content_orig:
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions , groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France , Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

articles.title_orig: Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
articles.title_zh: Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
articles.content_orig:
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the riots’ chief instigator and leader of the far-left La France Insoumise (LFI), is currently ranked second in most presidential polls. Marine Le Pen remains the favourite despite her continuing legal problems.
But the polls do not reveal Mélenchon’s strategy, his organisation, his coherence or his ruthlessness. It has become fashionable to dismiss his chances. He is too radical, they say, too inflammatory. As if that has not benefited other modern underdogs.
Born in Tangier in 1951, the former socialist schoolteacher became a senator at 35 and briefly served as a minister under the former PM Lionel Jospin. Mélenchon has spent the past 18 years building a party in his own image. This is his fourth presidential run, and there has been steady progress: in 2022 he came within a point and a half of the second round.
Mélenchon is quite obviously brilliant. Contrary to most other French politicians, who have the literacy of dried oysters, he is well-read and can speak well. He can cite Victor Hugo, whose parliamentary speeches he reveres as much as Les Misérables , as well as Robespierre and Michelet’s history of the Revolution. He is what the French call a tribun , a tribune, an orator, who regularly summons countless minions. His rally in June in Saint-Denis united tens of thousands of people.
Mélenchon has built a formidable political machine. It is hierarchical and motivated, possibly more so than any other party’s. In France, the trained ear can spot when his circle has held one of its internal strategy meetings: rumours start spreading, all using the same turns of phrase.
His team has adapted old-school Red methods to the modern world. Woe betide the victim of their online legions, who will barrage you with threats and insults for days. I was turned into a target after I allegedly argued for the expulsion of Algerian diplomats and the burning of their Paris embassy, following the incarceration of the writer Boualem Sansal.
Mélenchon’s lieutenants owe him every-thing and are quite ready to die for him. They are his Red Guard. First among equals is Manuel Bompard – doctor of applied mathematics, campaign director in 2017 and 2022, elected to his boss’s old seat in Marseille. He is the brains. Next comes Mathilde Panot. An international relations graduate from Sciences Po university, and now president of the parliamentary group, she is the enforcer, a woman who could credibly pass as a territorial and domineering 14th-century tavern keeper. Then there is Sophia Chik-irou, communications director and almost certainly in a relationship with Mélenchon (the leader of the Communist party has called LFI a sect under the spell of a couple).
Add to that the lower rungs, peopled with creatures of marsupial intelligence: National Assembly member Sébastien Delogu, the barely literate Marseille taxi driver whose only qualification is his cab licence; European Parliament member Rima Hassan, born in a Syrian refugee camp and turned ambassador to Gaza, who went on trial this week for glorifying terrorism; Raphaël Arnault, also in the National Assembly, who sits on a state security watchlist and co-founded the Jeune Garde. This is the outfit whose militants are under investigation for the death of 23-year-old Quentin Deranque, bludgeoned to oblivion in a Lyon street in February. Two of those charged with involvement were Arnault’s own parliamentary assistants.
Mélenchon has purged the party of any-one who isn’t deathly loyal. A number of old-timers, some of whom co-founded LFI with him, were ruthlessly cast out and blacklisted after an attempted modern leftist version of a marshals’ mutiny just before the snap election of 2024. The rebels told Mélenchon he was too tainted to be the party’s presidential nominee and should step aside. Five days later, most had official LFI candidates running against them, and their names were no longer mentioned by many former colleagues.
The rebels included my friend Alexis Corbière, an old companion of Mélenchon’s, who, despite the purge, managed to hold on to his seat in the Assembly. His experience featured prominently in a book on the brutality of LFI’s Stalinist tactics, entitled La Meute (‘The Pack’), which enjoyed considerable commercial success.
These lovely characters built LFI’s think-tank: the Institut la Boétie, founded in October 2019 by Bernard Pignerol, a councillor of state and an old friend of the boss. (Étienne de La Boétie wrote Discourse on Voluntary Servitude , a 16th-century essay explaining why whole peoples consent to serve one man…) It’s a facility with impressive political output – a stream of graduates from ten-weekend courses – financed by a million-euro grant from the party and tax-deductible donations which have been referred to the Treasury for scrutiny.
Woe betide the victim of their online legions, who will barrage you with threats and insults for days
Out of the Institut’s orbit come blue-haired ideologues and, far more dangerous, the sleeper agents: some 80 senior civil servants calling themselves the Phrygians, formed in May this year. They meet each month, co-ordinate by Telegram, and embed themselves at the finance ministry, the foreign ministry, the Banque de France and the European Commission. Their handler is the beautiful Clémence Guetté, who co-chairs the Institut with Mélenchon and runs the programme.
No other political family or faction in modern France is as well organised as LFI. This is one hell of a tight ship. I would willingly grant that their presidential prospects are poor for this cycle. But I would not be so bold as to dismiss their chances entirely.
LFI has something no other party seems able to hold on to: a disciplined strategy for attaining and keeping power. They have bet everything on Islam and its representatives, abandoning the workers of old in favour of immigrants and their descendants.
Sixty-nine per cent of French Muslims voted for Mélenchon in the first round of 2022. It is a bloc more cohesive than any other group voting for anyone, anywhere (he scored 88 per cent in some areas). If demographic curves are to be believed – which they are – this is bound to be a winning strategy, if not next year, then soon.
But Mélenchon would also be wise not to trust in his own invincibility. He may yet be consumed by his new friends, who have proven, on more than one occasion, perfectly willing to devour their own.

articles.title_orig: Meta Offers Zuckerberg New Shares to Keep Him in California
articles.title_zh: Meta Offers Zuckerberg New Shares to Keep Him in California
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg enters the debate on AI regulation, arguing against slowing down development. National Review columnist Caroline Downey analyzes his stance on safety oversight and independent evaluators.
Mark Zuckerberg has reached an agreement with Meta to remain in California after raising the possibility of leaving the state amid concerns over a proposed billionaire wealth tax.
Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO , previously told the company he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because of Proposition 40, a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of net worth on billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026, if approved.
Under the agreement, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares that he could sell to help cover a potential wealth tax bill in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California , or the state where Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, according to Reuters.
Zuckerberg, the world's sixth-richest person with a net worth approaching $250 billion, according to Forbes, could face a substantial tax bill that might require him to sell company shares.
MARK RUFFALO CALLS GAVIN NEWSOM'S BILLIONAIRE TAX STANCE 'DISQUALIFYING' AHEAD OF CALIFORNIA VOTE
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reached an agreement with the company that could allow him to cover a potential California billionaire wealth tax bill while maintaining voting control, according to Reuters. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images / Getty Images)
If passed by voters in November, the tax would be due in 2027, although payments could be spread over five years at an additional cost. Real estate, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Zuckerberg can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up voting control, according to Reuters.
Meta said Wednesday that it planned to issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027 to help fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control of the company.
In a statement provided to FOX Business, Meta pointed to comments from Chief Financial Officer Susan Li, who said the new shares were designed to help the company raise capital, compensate employees and pursue acquisitions while preserving its existing voting structure.
REAGAN ECONOMIST WARNS BILLIONAIRE TAX WOULD â€˜DESTROYâ€™ CALIFORNIA
Supporters hold signs advocating for the Billionaire Tax Now coalition during a news conference in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, April 27, 2026. (Caroline Brehman/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"We created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders," Li said during Meta's third-quarter earnings call.
Meta also said the decision followed a unanimous recommendation from a special committee of independent directors, which concluded that the new stock class would help finance the company's growth and preserve Zuckerberg's leadership.
According to a company filing, the committee emphasized the importance of Zuckerberg remaining in California to maintain close coordination with Meta's management and proximity to its Superintelligence Labs.
Although the ballot measure has been endorsed by the California Democratic Party, some prominent Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom , have opposed it.
Economist Art Laffer, a former economic adviser to President Ronald Reagan, previously warned that the measure could accelerate an exodus of California's wealthiest residents.
META ORDERED TO PAY $25B AFTER JURY FINDS IT MISLED USERS ON DATA PRIVACY
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg could sell newly issued non-voting shares to help cover a potential tax bill if California voters approve a proposed billionaire wealth tax. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"No one would want to go there to build their wealth only to be faced with this type of tax. It would cause an exodus of billionaires, which have not left California because the income taxes do not affect the billionaires much at all. This tax would really affect them," Laffer said.
California entrepreneur Eric Schiffer, chairman of the family office Patriarch and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, previously told FOX Business that passage of the measure could prompt wealthy entrepreneurs to leave California.
"I think the impact of this passing in California is a giant sucking sound of all of these entrepreneurs being sucked out of California because they're just not going to want to stay," Schiffer said.
California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) said "some billionaires" may decide to leave the state in response to the tax, potentially reducing the income tax revenue they generate.

articles.title_zh: Trump-sanctioned ICC wins EU Parliament’s human rights prize
articles.content_orig:
STRASBOURG — The International Criminal Court has won this year's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, awarded by the European Parliament, according to two people with knowledge of the decision.
The €50,000 prize honors defenders of human rights and freedom of thought, with past winners including Nelson Mandela, Alexei Navalny, Belarusian journalists, and the people of Ukraine.
Parliament President Roberta Metsola announced the decision later on Thursday: “The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the Court in upholding international law and justice.”
The Socialists and Democrats group nominated the ICC following U.S. President Donald Trump's sanctions on the court, announced on Oct. 9.
Inside the room, European People's Party chief Manfred Weber was counting on the right-wing groups to back his group's pick for the prize, Tanzanian politician Tundu Lissu — but needed the Patriots’ support to secure a majority. The Patriots, however, stood by their own nominees, the Iranian twin sisters imprisoned for protesting, one of whom has been sentenced to death.
Weber first asked the right-wing ECR to lobby Patriots chief Kinga Gál. When that failed, he approached her himself, according to two officials, granted anonymity to speak about the internal process. Gál ultimately recused herself from voting, allowing the Socialists, Renew, Greens and The Left to prevail with a relative majority of votes.
"It is a great achievement for the European Socialists that we led this proposal despite the EPP’s opposition. We are on the right side of history. This vote shows that the majority of this Parliament, together with our group, stands with international law,” Spanish S&D lawmaker Hana Jalloul, one of the promoters of the ICC nomination, told POLITICO.
French MEP Chloé Ridel said: "This is a message of hope and resistance sent to Donald Trump. No, we will not abandon the rule of law and international justice. We will stand with the ICC for as long as it takes.”
The prize is named in honor of Andrei Sakharov, a Soviet physicist and political dissident. Shortlisted candidates are traditionally invited to the Parliament’s award ceremony, which takes place during the December plenary session in Strasbourg. The Parliament plans in the coming months to increase the prize money from €50,000 to €100,000, according to an internal note seen by POLITICO.

The issue involves a retaining clip connecting the fuel tubes between the tank and engine. If the clip becomes lifted, the connection could allow fuel to leak from the resin tube attached to the fuel tank.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neocloud firms is "off the charts," but scarce capital is holding back growth.
"If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, adding that capabilities are "extraordinary."
"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said.
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.
Power is a major constraint for the AI boom, particularly in Europe, where electricity prices are higher . Huang said that the allocation of energy — which is scarce in the region — to companies like Nebius and Mistral is crucial for their growth.
"You can bring investments into Europe, but you have to start with having your own infrastructure," Huang explained. "If the neoclouds in Europe are able to establish an infrastructure here, then you can build the AI ecosystem, the AI economy on top of them, and then the flywheel of the AI economy will start in Europe. It will terminate in Europe."
He added: "Across all of Europe, you're going to need a lot more neoclouds."
Neocloud stocks such as CoreWeave and Nebius have been selling off recently as concerns grow over how much companies are spending on the AI infrastructure buildout, with the return on investments set to take longer than expected.
Investors are also wary of how much debt CoreWeave , one of the biggest neocloud players, is using to fund its data center buildout.
Neocloud stocks were lower in premarket trading on Thursday, with Nebius down 3.6%, and CoreWeave 4% lower. Iren and Applied Digital also shed nearly 4%.
Huang has been on a European media blitz this month as the chip giant looks to expand investments in the region's AI sector. The company has committed nearly $10 billion towards companies, universities, and research institutions.
While visiting London last week , Nvidia announced a stake worth over $1 billion in five U.K. startups. The chip giant is also investing in various French startups.
"We're trying to kickstart the AI economy in Europe," Huang told CNBC. "Europe has a tremendous amount of technology, tremendous amount of industrial know-how, incredible science and technology, and it's ready to engage and build the AI economy here."

articles.title_orig: Atari Is Officially Pulling Support for the Atari VCS
articles.title_zh: Atari Is Officially Pulling Support for the Atari VCS
articles.content_orig:
It's official! Atari is sunsetting the Atari VCS. Initially teased during E3 2017 under the name 'Ataribox' , the Linux-based "computer in a box" was the company's first console in decades and featured a design that was essentially a streamlined version of the Atari 2600. It was officially revealed the following year, during the 2018 Game Developer's Conference, with the company turning to crowdfunding to make the console a reality , raising roughly $3 million from 8,471 backers.
Delayed several times during its production, the machine eventually started shipping out to backers in December 2020, and was released in Australia, New Zealand and North America the following year. Early reviews, however, weren't exactly glowing , with the console also underperforming in terms of retail sales.
To add insult to injury, in a 2024 interview with Time Extension , Atari CEO Wade Rosen (who inherited the project from Atari's previous leadership) implied the company wouldn't have released it under its current leadership . Although Rosen insisted at the time that Atari was committed to supporting the platform into the future with new firmware updates and content for those who had invested in the console.
According to the company's website , Atari ended direct sales of the console the following year, and has since revealed plans to sunset support for the console as well, as of earlier this week.
In the statement released on the Atari Club Discord on Wednesday, October 23rd 2026, the Atari VCS team stated the VCS had "earned its rightful spot alongside the many console platforms Atari has launched over the past 50-plus years," before revealing it is planning to shut down the VCS store on February 1st, 2027.
As part of this move, it announced its intentions to release an OS update that "allows users to migrate all functionality to their local machine", removing "any dependencies on Atari infrastructure for authentication and software", and also said it will be pushing the Atari Home Brew app to all users, so developers can continue to support the VCS and share their creations with the community independently.
"Early next year we will post information that walks you through this OS migration, and the Home Brew App functionality, so everyone has plenty of time to prepare," the VCS team wrote. "We recognise that this is unwelcome news. We are working hard to ensure that the community can continue to use their VCS well into the future, and we are committed to supporting you through this transition."
What do you make of this news? Are you disappointed to see VCS support coming to an end? Or do you think Atari is right to finally move on from the device? Let us know your thoughts!

articles.title_orig: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
articles.title_zh: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
articles.content_orig:
The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X . Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion . (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications .
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.
One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy . If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.
Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.
The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

The iPhone Duo comes out tomorrow but, given the strong pre-order demand, it is already looking to be a smash hit. And we are all expecting Apple to follow up with a second-generation model next fall, which means the company has to be already working on the next-gen hardware.
On his Power On podcast , Mark Gurman reports that iPhone Duo 2 prototypes inside Apple include Face ID, with the Face ID sensor being integrated beneath the display on the outer screen.
The shift from Face ID to Touch ID on this phone was one of the biggest complaints raised by early iPhone Duo reviewers. 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller called it “the hardest thing to get used to” with the new foldable.
For the first-gen iPhone Duo, fitting Face ID inside the super-thin enclosure seemed to be the blocker. But Apple has been working on making Face ID smaller and less obtrusive, as seen with the under-display IR camera on the iPhone 18 Pro.
With iPhone Duo 2 and the twentieth anniversary iPhone Pro, we may see another evolution where both the IR camera and the flood illuminator go behind the screen, allowing the bezel or Dynamic Island cutout to be even smaller still.
Obviously, that just because they are testing the technology on iPhone Duo prototypes right now, it is not guaranteed that it will ship in next year’s revision. But it seems like that is what Apple is aiming for, so customers can probably expect it either next year or as part of the iPhone Duo 3, if development slips.
On the same episode, Gurman also says that employees have been exploring ways to also bring the Action button to a next-generation model of iPhone Duo as well, although he seems less confident about this.
It’s also unclear if Apple would remove the Touch ID sensor from the power button if it adds Face ID to the device, or whether it would keep both methods of biometrics allowing users to authenticate whether they are looking at the inner or outer display.

articles.title_zh: China Stocks Set for Bear Market as AI Trade, Policy Hopes Fade
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title_orig: France’s Debt Crisis Deepens as Foreign Investors Look for the Exit
articles.title_zh: France’s Debt Crisis Deepens as Foreign Investors Look for the Exit
articles.content_orig:
The yield on France's benchmark 10-year government bond briefly crossed the 5% threshold for the first time since 2002 on Wednesday, as the country grapples with multiple crises. Mass civil unrest resulted in a swathe of violent protests and rioting over the weekend, amid broad public dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the French government is struggling to pass a federal budget through a divided parliament as market pressure for significant fiscal consolidation mounts in response to a swelling national debt and wide deficit.
The yield on the 10-year OAT was last seen around 6 basis points higher at 4.9794%, after rising above 5% shortly before 11:30 a.m. in Paris (5:30 a.m. ET).
Financial markets have been piling pressure on France to fix its finances, with investors concerned that a politically fractured parliament will struggle to agree on the spending cuts required to bring down the country's ballooning deficit and national debt.
Lawmakers are in the process of negotiating the 2027 fiscal budget, with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu saying he will target 54 billion euros ($60.6 billion) in spending cuts.
France is currently subject to the EU's excessive deficit procedure , with the bloc recommending Paris bring its national deficit closer to 3% of GDP, compared with the 5.1% reached at the end of last year.
Budget talks have become a source of major political turbulence for France in recent years. After failing to reach a breakthrough in last year's negotiations, Lecornu used emergency legislation to force this year's budget through without parliamentary approval in February.
French finance minister Roland Lescure told French radio station RTL on Wednesday that the government was willing to bypass parliament again, if necessary, to force next year's budget through.
Speaking to French radio station RTL on Wednesday, Lescure said he was confident a budget would be passed within the allotted timeframe.
"I'm convinced of this because we have no choice," he said. "We have the tools to get it passed, so I'm convinced we'll succeed."
He noted that the government has "guardrails" available to it to force the budget through, including Article 49.3 of the French constitution, which allows the Prime Minister to force the adoption of a bill through the National Assembly without a vote.
"If we veer off course, we'll activate the guardrails," he told RTL.
Previous administrations were ousted when spending disagreements came to a head. Lecornu himself resigned less than a month into his tenure over budget divisions, only to be reappointed by President Emmanuel Macron days later.
But complicating the government's efforts to bring the French deficit under control are widespread protests that have turned increasingly violent since starting as a Parisian student movement last month. The unrest culminated in rioting and looting over the weekend, with officials estimating that the damages could be worth hundreds of millions of euros.
Bond traders are also looking ahead to next spring's French presidential election as a potential source of further instability. Current frontrunner, right-wing candidate Marine Le Pen, said earlier this month that she could bring the deficit below 3% within 18 months of being elected, but critics have questioned whether her proposed savings are credible.

The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk , the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, ​and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good ​idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion , putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks , depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab , a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype , which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars . Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla . That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

articles.title_zh: Space Debris Found Twice Within Days Amid ‘Growing Casualty Risk’
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia rocket debris? Image credit: BRIN
When it rains space debris.
Two cases of suspected Chinese rocket debris have been reported, in Indonesia and in the United States.
Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) reports that several bits of debris crashed into an oil palm plantation in Sampit, East Kotawaringin, Central Kalimantan.
BRIN researcher, Thomas Djamaluddin, said the object found on October 19 was a fragment of a Chinese ZhuQue-2E (ZQ-2E) rocket. There is a ZQE code associated with the ZhuQue-2E rocket, he adds.
There is a ZQE code associated with the ZhuQue-2E rocket. Image credit: BRIN
The rocket was developed by LandSpace, a Chinese commercial space startup and departed from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on October 14, 2026, carrying ten satellites.
Minnesota object. Image credit: Stevens County Sheriff’s Office
Yet another incident of possible space junk took place on October 14, 2026, at approximately 3:30pm, the Stevens County Sheriff’s Office in Minnesota received a phone call of foreign debris that was found in a cornfield in Scott Township.
“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” reports the sheriff’s office.
The Minnesota duty officer was notified of this and federal agencies responded.
“The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field. Agency officials have determined that there is no danger to the public due to this incident,” the office stated in a press release.
In a twisted bit of irony, the Minnesota debris may also be associated with a LandSpace Zhuque-2E rocket. According to Ars Technica , it could be tied to the rocket’s upper stage, hardware launched from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on September 15.
In both cases – Sampit and Scott Township — the recovered fragments are being examined to help identify their origin.

articles.title_orig: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.title_zh: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv killed one person and injured 24 others, including 4 children. Strikes damaged metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, an ambulance station, six emergency vehicles, homes and businesses.
Russian forces launched successive waves of ballistic missiles and attack drones against Kyiv overnight into Thursday, Oct. 22, killing one and injuring at least 24 people, including four children, and damaging a metro bridge, an ambulance station, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure across the Ukrainian capital.
Initially, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported in a Telegram update Thursday morning that the number of injured had risen from six to 15, including two 15-year-old children.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported at 7:55 a.m. that one person had been killed and 22 others injured, including four children, in Russian attacks on the capital.
In a statement issued at 9:21 a.m., the Kyiv City Military Administration said that 24 people had been injured, 16 of whom had been hospitalized.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kyiv starting on the evening of Oct. 21, causing fires and damage, the DSNS said:
Dniprovskyi district: One person was killed, and a child was hospitalized. Homes and vehicles were damaged, while residential and non-residential buildings caught fire. Five other people were injured.
Darnytskyi district: Transport infrastructure was damaged. No injuries were reported.
Sviatoshynskyi district: A non-residential building and a restaurant complex caught fire. The blaze, which covered 1,100 square meters, has been extinguished.
Obolonskyi district: Non-residential buildings were damaged, and fires broke out. Two people were injured. The fires have been extinguished.
Pecherskyi district: Buildings, ambulances and a monastery were damaged. Eight people were injured, including three children.
Holosiivskyi district: Six people were injured when a non-residential building was struck.
The overnight bombardment also damaged metro infrastructure on Kyiv’s  South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, prompting traffic restrictions on a key crossing over the Dnipro River.
In the central Pecherskyi district, Russian strikes damaged an ambulance station and six emergency medical vehicles, according to the mayor.
The latest attack marks another assault on essential civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, with Russian missiles hitting residential neighborhoods, transport facilities and emergency medical services.
The Russian bombardment also struck part of the capital’s metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, a major crossing connecting Kyiv’s two banks.
“As a result of the shelling, part of the metro infrastructure on the South Bridge was damaged,” Klitschko reported on Telegram .
The Kyiv City Military Administration announced traffic restrictions on the bridge in the direction from the right bank to the left bank because of the attack.
The bridge carries both road traffic and a section of Kyiv’s green metro line across the Dnipro.
Damage to the crossing adds pressure to Kyiv’s transport network as the capital faces repeated Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Russian strikes also damaged an emergency medical facility in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district.
Klitschko confirmed that the damaged building was an ambulance station and that six ambulances had also sustained damage.
No medical personnel were injured, the mayor said.
The damage to emergency medical services came as ambulances and rescue crews were responding to casualties elsewhere in the capital.
The overnight strikes also sparked a fire at a restaurant building in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that the fire broke out following the Russian attack, adding another civilian site to the growing list of damaged properties.
Earlier Wednesday evening, Russian missiles struck residential buildings and businesses in Dniprovskyi district.
Klitschko reported direct hits on a vehicle repair workshop and a private residential building, while debris damaged another house.
Emergency crews were dispatched amid concerns that people could be trapped beneath the rubble.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell near a gas station, causing additional damage.
In Darnytskyi district, a Russian strike hit the grounds of a transport infrastructure facility, according to the mayor.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings as Russian ballistic missiles approached the capital late Wednesday and after midnight Thursday.
The warnings began during Wednesday evening’s assault, when explosions were reported across Kyiv.
Further ballistic missile threats followed after midnight, including warnings shortly after 12 a.m. and another at approximately 12:31 a.m.
The Air Force also tracked Russian attack drones approaching the Kyiv region and subsequently warned of a drone over the capital.
The successive threats forced residents to remain in shelters as emergency crews responded to damage across multiple districts.
Russian forces launched a massive combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine beginning at 6 p.m. on Oct. 21, targeting Kyiv as the primary strike location, the Ukrainian Air Force reported.
The attack involved Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, Zircon and Oniks missiles, and 210 strike drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya (Parody) decoy drones.
“The primary target of the strike was Kyiv,” the report said.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian Air Force aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
As of 9 a.m. on Thursday, preliminary data showed that Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 181 Russian drones, including 87 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones and other types.
“Ten strike drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! Do not ignore air raid alerts!” the Air Force warned at 9.01 a.m.
Russian weapons struck 32 locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at eight other locations.
The latest strikes came amid renewed US-led diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
On Wednesday, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg after holding discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European officials earlier in the week.
The Kremlin subsequently signaled willingness to resume trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
However, Moscow has not abandoned its territorial claims or its opposition to Ukraine joining NATO.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly stressed that any negotiated settlement must include reliable security guarantees to prevent renewed Russian aggression.

articles.title_orig: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.title_zh: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures rose 2.68% to $111.74 a barrel as of 6:30 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained 2.21% to $99.30.
The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.
The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.
He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.
"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.

articles.title_orig: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
articles.title_zh: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating.
Bukele, known for his intense crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador, warned in Wednesday’s statement that a more forceful response was coming if the personnel were not released alive and well.
“Do not take our word for empty threats,” the president wrote, addressing the gangs allegedly responsible for holding the four men. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.”
Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle carrying the men three days earlier, in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country last year.
The four men, aviation technicians with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s government issued a news release on Wednesday evening saying the release of the abducted soldiers was an “absolute priority”.
It was not immediately clear if Haitian authorities received any confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.
The government said a meeting was held at the prime minister’s office “to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force”.
A spokesperson for the GSF did not immediately respond to a message seeking details
The UN-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday’s attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops, which comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador is among several countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form part of the gang suppression force, with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.
Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January through mid-September this year, and more than 230 have been kidnapped, according to the UN.
The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs, including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitel’Homme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou.
Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and the US.
